rationale: A wins because it keeps the story inside the facts and still finds four real lanes; "Eight Sleep's mattress now tracks blood oxygen and snoring. It won't call the result a diagnosis." is the cleanest reporter-shaped angle in the batch. B has useful instincts, but it decorates too much: "sleep apnea, which affects tens of millions of adults, most undiagnosed" and "FDA warning letters" are not in the update and turn a sharp regulatory question into a liability. A also gives better kill criteria, especially "Without the clinic on record, it is a press-release line and should not go out."
gaps_in_A: The category angle headline, "Sleep trackers tell you that you snored. This bed changes its temperature while you are doing it," risks implying a direct response to snoring before the update proves the trigger logic.

The athlete/biohacker fact is included under the category angle, but A wisely avoids overclaiming; it still misses a possible buyer-mismatch angle around marketing to athletes while shipping sleep-apnea-adjacent signals.
The clinic angle is honest but thin; it needs the named clinic in the angle copy, because the update says one exists.
gaps_in_B: Invented epidemiology: "sleep apnea, which affects tens of millions of adults, most undiagnosed" may be broadly true, but it was not supplied and changes the stakes of the pitch.
Overheated legal/regulatory claim: "the exact fact pattern that draws FDA warning letters" is a serious assertion with no evidence in the update.
Invented price precision: "On a $3,000 mattress" turns "several thousand dollars" into a specific number the update did not give.
Fake specificity in outlet shape: naming "STAT News, KHN, Wired Health" and "Undark, Science" substitutes brand names for a tighter sub-beat and risks sending this to the wrong desk.
